title: How do you solve a growth case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete growth case guide: sorting and sizing every option, worked through a gym chain's 20% revenue target, plus mistakes and practice prompts.
hook: You solve a growth case by sorting the options into a clear structure, sizing the biggest ones, and showing whether they add up to the client's target, then sequencing them by speed, cost and risk. Listing ideas is the trap; sizing them is the answer. This guide works through a gym chain's 20% revenue target with every number shown.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet a growth case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example: a gym chain grows 20%
  • Breaking revenue into its drivers
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

When you will meet a growth case

The client wants more revenue and is open to options: "how can we double sales in five years?", "where should we grow next?", "how do we get more subscribers?" Unlike a profitability case, nothing is broken, so there is no single cause to find. The task is to choose among many possible moves, which is why structure and sizing matter so much.

The structure, and the first question to ask

Pin down the target and the limits first:

How much growth, by when? Which parts of the business grow today, and is anything off the table, such as acquisitions or new countries?

Then sort the options by how far they move from what the client already does. This is the logic of the Ansoff matrix, expressed in plain terms:

  • Existing products, existing customers. Sell more to the people you already serve: more visits, bigger orders, higher prices, better retention.
  • Existing products, new customers. New cities, new segments, new channels.
  • New products, existing customers. Extra services or products for the same people.
  • New products, new customers. Diversification, often through an acquisition.

Risk rises as you move down the list. Size each option, check the total against the target, then say how you would deliver each one: build it, partner or buy. The growth framework covers each quadrant in more depth.

A fully worked example: a gym chain grows 20%

The prompt: a gym chain wants to grow revenue by 20% in three years, from $50M to $60M. How? The figures are illustrative.

Step 1: understand today's revenue

100,000 members × $35 a month × 12 = $42M from memberships, plus $8M from personal training and extras. Total: $50M. The gap to close is $10M.

Step 2: sort and size the options

OptionWorkingExtra revenue
Raise the monthly fee by $2100,000 × $2 × 12$2.4M
Open 10 new gyms10 × 1,500 members × $35 × 12$6.3M
Grow personal training and extras by a fifth$8M × 20%$1.6M
Total$10.3M (about 21%)

The three options just clear the target, with little to spare. Say so: if any one falls short, the client misses.

Step 3: test each option

  • Price rise. $2 is a 5.7% increase. Revenue still rises unless more than about 5.4% of members cancel because of it: 94,600 members at $37 bring in about the same as 100,000 at $35. Ask how members reacted to past rises.
  • New gyms. Each brings in 1,500 × $35 × 12 = $630k a year once full. If one costs $1M to open and runs at a 35% margin, it earns about $220k a year and pays back in about 4.5 years. New gyms also take time to fill, so not all $6.3M will arrive within three years, and gyms near existing ones may cannibalise them.
  • Extras. Cheap to test: better trainer scheduling, packages sold at sign-up. A 20% lift is ambitious, so treat it as an upside.

Step 4: the recommendation

The $10M target is reachable with three moves worth about $10.3M together: ten new gyms ($6.3M), a $2 fee rise ($2.4M) and more personal training ($1.6M). There is little headroom, so I'd start the fast, cheap moves now: test the price rise in a few gyms, and push training packages at sign-up. In parallel, I'd pick sites for new gyms away from existing ones, since they are the biggest lever but take the longest to fill. The main risk is the new gyms ramping up too slowly, so I'd also look for a fourth option as a buffer.

Breaking revenue into its drivers

Another way to find growth is to split revenue into its drivers and ask which one can move. A meal-kit company has 100,000 active customers placing two orders a month at $30 each: 100,000 × 2 × $30 × 12 = $72M a year. It wants $90M, a 25% rise, without raising prices.

  • More customers: 110,000 at the same frequency gives $79.2M.
  • More orders: those 110,000 ordering 2.2 times a month gives about $87.1M.
  • Bigger baskets: $31 per order instead of $30 takes it to about $90.0M.

No single lever gets there, but three modest moves do. Each still needs evidence, and growth bought with discounts can destroy profit: if new customers cancel after one cheap box, they never repay the cost of signing them up. Check contribution and acquisition cost for each initiative, and look at whether customers who order twice go on to order a third time. Our unit economics explainer shows how.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer is a brainstorm:

They could open new gyms, add classes, launch an app, sell protein shakes, partner with employers, go abroad and run more marketing.

A strong answer sizes and sequences:

Let me size the three biggest options and check whether they reach the $10M gap.
New gyms are the biggest lever, but slowest and riskiest, so I'd sequence them after the quick wins.

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Listing ideas without sizing or priority. Size the top three; ignore the long tail.
  2. Not checking the total against the target. Add it up and say whether it gets there.
  3. Ignoring cost and risk. The biggest option is not always the best. Compare payback and speed.
  4. Chasing revenue at the expense of profit. Growth bought with heavy discounts or high acquisition costs can make the client poorer.
  5. Forgetting the side effects. More customers can mean more churn, and new sites or products can cannibalise old ones.

Practise with these prompts

Should a coffee chain sell its beans in supermarkets?

Show the answer
  • Market: size of premium coffee in supermarkets; competitors and shelf space.
  • Economics: price, the retailer's margin, our cost; volume needed to pay back.
  • Cannibalisation and halo: café visits lost against new customers and brand awareness gained.
  • Brand and operations: a premium image on a shelf next to discounts; roasting and supply capacity.

Where to start: net profit after the café visits the client might lose.

The trap: ignoring the effect on café visits and on a premium brand.

How should a newspaper grow digital subscriptions?

Show the answer
  • Reach: traffic from search, social and newsletters; new audiences and topics.
  • Conversion: paywall design, trials, price, sign-up friction.
  • Retention: reading habits, apps, bundles; cancellation and win-back.
  • Revenue per subscriber: tiers, family plans, annual against monthly billing.

Where to start: the funnel. Find the step with the biggest drop-off.

The trap: listing marketing ideas without the reach, convert, retain funnel.

How can a university attract more international students?

Show the answer
  • Markets: which countries have demand; competition from universities in other countries.
  • Offer: courses, fees, scholarships, rankings, graduate jobs.
  • Recruitment: agents, partner institutions, digital; conversion from offer to arrival.
  • Barriers: visa policy, housing and support.

Where to start: conversion from offer to arrival, since many offers are lost to visas and rival universities.

The trap: ignoring visas and housing, which often cap numbers.
